titleStmt.title: No. 922
The Secretary of State to Certain Diplomatic and Consular Offices

div.head:
No. 922
The Secretary of State to Certain Diplomatic and Consular Offices
div.p: Top Secret
CA–3378. Subject: Arab-Israel Settlement.

The purpose of this instruction is to solicit the assistance of the addressees in working out the elements of a final settlement of the Arab-Israel problem and in determining the most effective tactics to this end, including timing. To serve as a starting point, certain preliminary views developed in NEA are set forth.

It should be made clear at the start that we are under no illusions as to the complexities of the problem the emotions present and the basic conflicts of interest. NIE 36–54 on “Probable Developments
in the Arab States” of September 7, 1954 states “Arab leaders are likely to be extremely cautious about offending public feeling on the Israeli question and will probably not be willing for some time to risk negotiation and compromise on the most important issues. . . They will refuse to meet with Israel for the purpose of negotiating outstanding issues unless Israel meets conditions—acceptance of existing UN resolutions as a basis for negotiation—which the Arabs are reasonably sure Israel will never agree to. In dealing with specific problems in Arab-Israeli relations short of a formal peace settlement some Arab leaders have recently appeared less intransigent. . . The Israelis have not, however, shown a like tendency to reasonableness and compromise.” However, an ideal time to seek a comprehensive settlement will probably never arrive and the present appears to us as propitious a moment as is likely to occur in the foreseeable future. Also, the attempt at least will stimulate thinking in terms of a settlement, and show how far we may expect to go in the short term. In addition, the elements of a settlement developed may serve as a goal towards which to work.

The general objective sought may be described as: To bring about a transition from the present armistice regime governing relations between the Arab states and Israel to formal peace and concurrent agreements on settlements of issues remaining from the Palestine conflict to the maximum extent feasible in a span of two years; the effort to be carried out in a manner not unduly jeopardizing other US area objectives (notably area defense arrangements) and without the employment of unusual measures (i.e., economic sanctions or armed force).
The basic obstacles to be overcome in attaining this objective appear to be:

list.item: 1. The unwillingness of Israel to accept a status as a finite Middle Eastern state; and the insistence of Israel on a special role as the center of a world-wide “nation” of Jewry. Prime Minister Sharett’s speech before the Knesset on November 15, carried in the FBIS of November 16, is of particular interest in this regard.
2. The unwillingness of the Arab states to accept the permanent existence of an Israel, which they fear is intent on expansion.

div.p: The specific objectives which we might strive for at an optimum are:

list.item: 1. Formal peace between Israel on the one hand and Egypt, Jordan and Lebanon on the other. (Settlements involving Syria, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and perhaps Iraq may prove even more difficult to obtain during the two year period.)
2. Permanent recognized boundaries for Israel after frontier rectifications.
3. Security on the border and cooperation in control of infiltration.
4. Termination of the Suez Canal blockade and of the Arab secondary boycott.
5. Agreements on repatriation and resettlement of refugees, with some implementation.
6. Agreement on compensation.
8. A “Free Port” at Haifa for Jordan and free routes across Israel linking Egypt, Jordan and Lebanon.
9. Agreement on the Unified Development of the Jordan Valley.
We recognize that even if successful, we would be faced still with the implementation of many of the agreements reached, particularly those concerned with the refugees.

div.p: Concurrently, we would endeavor to progress on area defense arrangements through a series of bilaterals linking certain Arab states (especially Iraq) to Turkey and Pakistan. Success would contribute to an Arab-Israel settlement by instilling in the Arab states a greater sense of security and by deflecting their concentration on Israel. We would hope to expand the defense arrangements to provide for the effective use of Israel’s armed forces. Whether it could be done within the two year period under consideration is questionable.

The prospects for the enterprise will be affected, of course, to a considerable degree by the inducements which may be held out by the US and other cooperating powers, especially the UK and Turkey. Among those which the US might extend are:

list.item: 1. Continuation of our present policy of impartiality, especially continued refusal to be guided by Israel’s unrealistic insistence that she be considered a favored bastion of Western civilization in the Middle East and as the center of world-wide nation of “Jewry.”

2. Within the limitations of our constitutional processes, a firm public undertaking, to be given as part of a final settlement, that the US will use force if necessary to prevent alterations by force of the boundaries established and to preserve the security of Israel and the Arab states against each other. (It has not been determined yet whether it would be practical for the US to extend such a guarantee or whether it would be advisable from a world-wide policy point of view.)
3. Grant economic assistance to the Arab states and Israel, expanded in some cases, plus continued aid to the refugees.
4. An enlarged program of grant military assistance to certain Arab states and also military assistance to Israel.

div.p: Our tentative thinking is that the best tactics would be a combination of our present step-by-step approach with an across-the-board effort directed originally at securing an Egyptian-Israel agreement and then a Jordan-Israel agreement, utilizing the Trieste technique. The aspects of the Trieste technique which appear pertinent to the present problem are: (1) presentation to the parties by third powers of suggestions for a settlement; (2) no direct meetings between the parties; (3) subsequently efforts by the third powers to reconcile the conflicting positions. We recognize that these tactics run counter to the Israel thesis of direct talks.

We believe the first approach should be made to Egypt because: (a) she is less concerned over Israel and more likely to move; (b) her example, as in the case of Bunche’s negotiations of the armistice agreements at Rhodes, would help induce the other Arab states to act; (c) the Suez Base Agreement and our aid programs place the US and UK in a particularly favorable position to influence Egypt; (d) simultaneous approaches to several Arab states would considerably increase the danger of publicity and of the Arabs uniting on an extreme stand.

We recall that the Arab League Council on April 1, 1950 voted to forbid any Arab state from negotiating or concluding a separate peace or a political, military or economic accord with Israel, and to expel any state which did so. The resolution was a product both of the war with Israel and of resentment, particularly Egyptian, at Jordan’s plans to annex Eastern Palestine. Some further action of the League may be required before an Egyptian-Israel settlement is finally signed, or Egypt may feel able to ignore the resolution as was done by Jordan in May 1950 when the Political Committee of the League declared that Jordan’s annexation of Arab Palestine was a violation of the resolution.
An illustrative time-table covering the first phase of our effort would read:

list.item: 1. Development with the UK of the elements of a solution and agreement on strategy—January 1955.
2. Discussions with Turkey, concentrating on the part we hope it will play in the concurrent approach to Middle East defense arrangements—January 1955.
3. Frank and full discussions with Prime Minister Nasir of Egypt—late February or March 1955.
4. Depending on Nasir’s receptivity, discussions with Israel—March or April 1955.
5. Approach to Jordan by the UK with the US in support role and with Egyptian support and advice if (as we hope) Egyptians show active interest in bringing about a settlement.

div.p:
After the initial approaches to Egypt and Israel and once the process of reconciling the two positions is under way, the utmost
flexibility would be maintained on the timing of approaches to the other Arab states. Although Egyptian views would be considered, they alone would not be allowed to control the timing of further moves.

As the addressees have been informed, we plan to determine with the UK in January the elements of a solution and tactics. Subsequently, we expect to work in the closest cooperation with the British. The problem of France gives us considerable concern since we feel her association with the venture would decrease its receptivity in the Arab states and yet, should she be excluded, France could exert considerable negative influence. It will probably prove advisable to keep her generally informed but we hope to avoid doing so at least until after the first approach to Egypt. We believe Turkey could play a particularly useful role in connection with the defense arrangements part of the over-all plan. As indicated in Deptel 548 to Ankara, we think it preferable for Turkey at present not to concern itself directly with the Arab-Israel problem. It will probably prove useful for Turkey to participate in any international commitment guaranteeing the final Arab-Israel boundaries. We would expect to keep the Turks informed of our thinking and of progress. Pakistan could possibly play a helpful part in connection with area defense arrangements.

The above line of thinking in NEA is highly tentative and should not be construed as a Departmental position. The views of the addressees on the entire problem are desired by despatch. It would be particularly helpful if, in addition to general thoughts, the reports covered the following:

1. The elements of a final settlement between the country of assignment and Israel, irrespective of assessments of the possibility of moving at this time. A detailed statement is desired referring where appropriate to the specific objectives set forth above.
2. The pros and cons of attempting an across-the-board settlement supplementing the present step-by-step approach.
3. General views on tactics including particularly the appropriateness of the Trieste technique.

list.item: a. Would approaches to individual Arab countries singly be preferable to simultaneous approaches to two or more of the Arab countries?
b. Under optimum conditions what timing would appear reasonable?
c. What would be the reaction if the initial approach is made through Egypt?
d. If Egypt did move towards a settlement, what would be the effect on the other Arab states of the Egyptian example and of Egyptian leadership?

div.p: 4. What inducements from the US, UK or other outside countries would be most effective in the country of assignment? If economic or military aid is recommended, general estimates of the magnitude and duration would be helpful.
5. The usefulness of endeavoring to move forward simultaneously on area defense arrangements.

list.item: a. How could efforts in this field most effectively assist in progress towards an Arab-Israel settlement.

note.p: Sent to Amman, Baghdad, Beirut, Cairo, Damascus, Jidda, Tel Aviv, and Jerusalem; repeated to London and Ankara.
The ellipses in the quotation appear in the source text.
